query: Design a system where an LLM-based assistant can autonomously manage a small e-commerce store's customer support: it should triage incoming tickets by intent (refund, tracking, product question, complaint), decide when to escalate to a human, use tools like an order lookup API and a refund processing API, and handle multi-turn conversations where it might need to gather info across several steps before resolving an issue. I want the full architecture—how the agent loop works, what the tool schemas look like, how memory/state is maintained between turns, and how you'd implement guardrails so it doesn't approve refunds above a certain threshold without human approval. Please include pseudocode for the core orchestration logic.

Our UniFi network spans 14 sites across three regional offices, and over the past year different team members have created separate markdown files documenting host inventories, device configs, VLAN assignments, and troubleshooting runbooks — but there's massive overlap and contradiction between them. I need you to first pull a current inventory of all hosts and devices across every UniFi site so we have an accurate baseline of what's actually deployed (include status, model, firmware, IP, and which site each belongs to), then take the 23 documentation files in our `/docs/infrastructure/` folder and consolidate them into a clean, non-redundant set. Merge the VLAN docs (there are four covering nearly the same content), combine the three overlapping troubleshooting guides, and unify the per-site inventory docs into one canonical source-of-truth document that reflects the live infrastructure data you just pulled. Make sure nothing valuable gets lost — some files have unique notes about firmware quirks or site-specific firewall rules that only appear once — but eliminate all the duplicated and outdated content.

We're building a developer education platform and I need help with three interconnected pieces. First, I'm creating a Zed editor extension in Rust that provides a custom `/webinar-notes` slash command — when invoked during a live coding webinar, it should pull the current webinar's agenda, talking points, and audience poll results from our Firestore backend and format them as contextual notes in the editor. The slash command needs to output structured markdown with engagement hooks (audience questions to pose, demo transition cues, and "aha moment" callouts) so the presenter can glance at it while live-coding. For the Firestore side, I need an async service layer in TypeScript that manages webinar documents (agenda items, real-time poll results, attendee engagement scores) with transactions to atomically update the engagement metrics as audience members interact, plus proper error handling for when the presenter's extension polls during high-traffic moments. The webinar narrative itself needs to build toward a climactic live refactoring demo — help me structure the arc so it starts with a relatable "legacy code pain" story, builds tension through incremental improvements, includes two interactive polling moments to keep the audience engaged, and lands on a satisfying reveal. Show me the full Rust extension code with the `run_slash_command` implementation, the Firestore service with transaction patterns, and the webinar flow document that ties them together.

I'm building a math-themed board game in Obsidian where two players take turns placing pieces on a hex grid to claim territory — no dice, no hidden info, pure strategy like Go meets Hex. I need three things: First, help me design the core mechanics, win conditions, and balance considerations so neither player has an overwhelming first-move advantage. Second, I want to visualize the scoring function for territory control as interactive Desmos graphs embedded in my Obsidian notes — specifically, I need parametric curves showing how the value of connected regions grows nonlinearly with size, and inequality shading to represent each player's dominated zones on a coordinate plane approximation of the board. Third, I want the game to have a soundtrack feature: write me an AppleScript that queries my Apple Music library for tracks in a "Board Games" playlist, shuffles them, and starts playback when I launch the game session, with the ability to shift to a different playlist called "Endgame Tension" when a player controls more than 60% of the board — I'll trigger that manually from a hotkey. Can you put together the game design document, the Desmos graph code blocks, and the AppleScript all in one cohesive Obsidian note?

Set up a new Deepnote workspace for our InsightPulseAI data team that organizes notebooks into exploration, scheduled ETL jobs, and Superset-ready summary table sections. We need a shared project configuration that includes pre-commit security hooks to prevent credential leaks, a standardized Claude-based framework structure for each notebook template, and auto-detection logic so the setup script can identify whether a notebook is using PySpark, pandas, or SQL-only and apply the right boilerplate accordingly. The summary tables should land in a `gold/` schema that Superset can query directly, and each job notebook needs a consistent header block with dataset lineage metadata. Can you generate the full setup scaffolding and the detection patterns for this?

Here's the draft blog post for Every's newsletter about our new AI-powered meal planning feature. Can you do a full line-by-line edit to make sure it follows our style guide (especially around comma usage, capitalization of product names, and our preferred tone), and also optimize it for the target keyword "AI meal planner" — check the heading hierarchy, meta title/description, keyword placement and density, and make sure readability scores are solid for search? I want it publish-ready on both fronts. Here's the draft:
---

**Title: Meet Your New AI Meal Planner: How Every Is Changing the Way You Eat**

**Subtitle: our new feature uses Artificial Intelligence to build personalized weekly meal plans in seconds.**

We're excited to announce that every has officially launched it's AI-powered meal planning tool — and it's a game-changer.

For years, meal planning has been one of those things that everyone knows they should do but nobody actually enjoys. Between dietary restrictions, budget constraints, and the eternal question of "what's for dinner?", planning your meals for the week can feel like a chore. That's where our new AI Meal Planner comes in.

## How the AI meal planner works

The AI Meal Planner uses advanced machine learning algorithms to analyze your preferences, dietary needs, and even what's on sale at your local grocery store. It then generates a fully customized weekly meal plan, complete with recipes and a consolidated shopping list. The AI meal planner learns from your feedback over time, getting smarter with every interaction.

## Why we built an ai meal planner

At Every, we believe technology should make everyday life easier. Our team spent over 18 months developing this feature, working closely with nutritionists and data scientists to make sure the recommendations are not only convenient, but also nutritionally balanced. We wanted to build an AI meal planner that actually understands real people's lives — not just calorie counts.

## Key features of Every's AI Meal Planner

- Personalized weekly Meal Plans based on your taste preferences
- Smart grocery lists that save you time, and money
- Integration with popular grocery delivery services
- Dietary filter support (Keto, vegan, gluten-free and more)
- Family-size scaling, so you can plan for 1 or 10

## Getting started is easy

Just open the Every app, navigate to the meal planning tab and let the AI Meal Planner do the rest. It's available to all Every Pro subscribers starting today.

We think this is going to fundamentally change the way you think about meal prep. Try it out and let us know what you think!

---

**Meta title:** AI Meal Planner | Every
**Meta description:** Every's new AI meal planning feature builds custom weekly meal plans. Try it today.

We have a custom PowerShell module (`BuildTools`) that packages our internal plugins for distribution — each plugin has a `hooks/` directory with `pre-install.ps1`, `post-install.ps1`, and `pre-uninstall.ps1` scripts that get bundled into the final `.nupkg`. Right now the packaging script (`Invoke-PluginPack.ps1`) silently continues when a hook script path is missing or malformed (e.g., contains spaces or special chars that break on Windows), and we've had production incidents where plugins shipped without their post-install hooks. I need three things: (1) Rewrite `Invoke-PluginPack.ps1` to properly validate all hook script paths, use `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` with proper try/catch/terminating error handling, and correctly resolve paths using `Resolve-Path` instead of string concatenation — watch out for the PowerShell `-and`/`-or` operator precedence pitfalls we keep hitting. (2) Design a test automation strategy for the entire plugin packaging pipeline — I want a Pester test suite structured as a proper test pyramid with unit tests for individual path validation functions, integration tests that actually invoke the packaging against a temp plugin fixture with all hook variants (missing hooks, hooks with spaces in paths, hooks with syntax errors), and a small set of end-to-end tests that can run in our Azure DevOps CI pipeline to verify the final `.nupkg` contains the correct hook entries. (3) Add a CI stage definition (YAML for Azure Pipelines) that runs the Pester tests on a Windows agent, gates the packaging step on test passage, and publishes test results. Make sure the Pester tests cover edge cases like UNC paths and the `-not (Test-Path ...)` vs `!(Test-Path ...)` behavioral difference in strict mode.

Our SaaS observability platform "Beacon" currently offers a free tier and a Pro plan. We're seeing strong adoption among DevOps teams who start with log aggregation but rarely discover our APM and distributed tracing modules. I need you to draft a product-led expansion playbook that maps out the journey from free-tier signup through Pro upgrade and then cross-sell/upsell into our APM add-on and Enterprise tier — include specific in-app triggers, usage thresholds, and email nurture touchpoints for each transition. Also, we just reorganized our monorepo and I need the playbook to reference the relevant codebases accurately: the usage-tracking event definitions live in `src/billing/events/`, the feature flag configs are in `config/feature-flags/`, the in-app messaging templates are at `frontend/src/components/nudges/`, and the email templates are under `marketing/emails/expansion-campaigns/`. Make sure every reference to these paths in the doc uses proper repo-relative formatting so engineers can click through from our GitHub-rendered markdown.

Our team just refactored the markdown rendering pipeline in our `docs-engine` repo and I noticed the PR description template we use has several broken relative links — things like `[Architecture Guide](docs/architecture.md)` and `[Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md)` that don't resolve properly on GitHub when people view the PR. I also want to update the `src/renderer/markdownParser.ts` file to handle GFM autolinks and reference-style links correctly, since right now it silently drops them. Can you validate and fix all the markdown links in our PR description template at `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` so they point to proper blob URLs on the `main` branch, and then propose the code changes needed in `markdownParser.ts` to support those link types? Show me the diffs and your reasoning for each change before anything gets merged.

We're building a PydanticAI agent that handles customer support ticket routing for our SaaS platform "HelpDesk Pro." The agent needs to look up customer subscription tiers from our PostgreSQL database, check their recent ticket history via our internal REST API, and fetch the current on-call engineer schedule from PagerDuty — all of which should be injected as dependencies rather than hardcoded. Can you set up the agent with a properly typed `deps_type` dataclass that bundles the async database pool, the HTTP client for our internal API, and the PagerDuty client, then show how to use `RunContext` to access each of these inside system prompt functions, tool functions, and result validators? I also want the deps to include the authenticated user's context (tenant ID, role, locale) so the agent can personalize responses. Please include the full agent definition, the dependency dataclass, a couple of tools that use `ctx.deps` to query the DB and call the APIs, and a `main()` that wires everything up with real async resource lifecycle management (opening/closing the DB pool and HTTP sessions properly).

We're building a collaborative project management tool called "TaskFlow" using Rails 7 and we need to implement live presence indicators and instant task status updates so that when one team member moves a card on the Kanban board or starts typing a comment, every other team member viewing the same board sees the change immediately without refreshing. Can you walk me through the full implementation — setting up the WebSocket connection, creating the appropriate channels for board-level and user-level streams, handling subscriptions on the JavaScript side with Stimulus controllers, and broadcasting task state changes from the model callbacks? We also need to handle edge cases like reconnection after network drops and ensuring that presence indicators correctly show users going offline. Our current stack is Rails 7 with esbuild, PostgreSQL, and Redis.

We have a Python SDK called `atlas-geo` for geospatial tile rendering that we're about to open-source. The package has about 30 public modules across `atlas_geo.layers`, `atlas_geo.projections`, `atlas_geo.tiles`, and `atlas_geo.styles` namespaces — all classes and functions already have Google-style docstrings with Args, Returns, Raises, and Examples sections. Can you generate a complete API reference in Markdown from those docstrings? I want one `.md` file per subpackage with a table of contents, all public classes and their methods documented with parameter types and descriptions, cross-links between related classes (e.g., `TileRenderer` references `Projection`), and a top-level `index.md` that gives an overview of the package architecture. Please also include usage examples pulled from the docstring `Examples` blocks formatted as fenced code blocks, and flag any public symbols that are missing docstrings so we can fix them before release.

We're redesigning the checkout flow for our "FreshCart" grocery delivery app (React Native + Node.js backend) and I need a comprehensive approach. First, search through our codebase to find all existing checkout-related components, API routes, and any A/B test configurations we currently have — I know there's a `CheckoutWizard`, some step components, and a cart validation service scattered across the monorepo but I'm not sure where everything lives. Then, using what you find in the code, I want you to evaluate our current multi-step checkout against Hick's Law and Fitts's Law — we're getting a 68% cart abandonment rate and I suspect the 7-step flow with tiny tap targets on mobile is killing us. Propose a redesigned flow using the Double Diamond process: map out the discovery/define/develop/deliver phases, apply MoSCoW prioritization to the proposed changes (we only have one sprint to ship an MVP improvement), and write user stories in proper "As a [user], I want [goal], so that [benefit]" format for the top-priority items. Also search our repo for any existing analytics or event tracking hooks so we can plan a proper usability testing checklist for the new flow. Finally, draft a lightweight PRD covering the problem statement, success metrics (targeting <45% abandonment), Kano Model classification of each proposed feature, and a RICE score for the top 5 changes so we can defend priorities to stakeholders.

We have an epic in our Jira backlog called "Veterinary Clinic Patient Portal" that covers everything from pet owners booking appointments online, viewing vaccination records, receiving medication reminders, messaging their vet, and paying invoices. The team estimated it at around 80 story points and it's way too large to pull into a sprint. Can you break this epic down into well-defined user stories with acceptance criteria for each? Please make sure each story is small enough to complete in a single sprint, follows the INVEST principles, and is written from the perspective of the appropriate persona (pet owner, veterinarian, or clinic receptionist). If any story still feels too big after the initial split, break it down further.

We have a Spring Boot integration test suite for our "InventorySync" warehouse management service that runs against a real PostgreSQL database using Testcontainers. Right now, our tests verify that inventory adjustments propagate correctly, but we want to expand coverage. Can you help me write a new test class that spins up a Postgres container, seeds it with component data fetched from the Sippy component readiness API (https://sippy.dptools.openshift.org/api/component_readiness/components), and then validates that our sync logic correctly maps each Sippy component name to an inventory category in our `component_mappings` table? The test should pull the live list of component names from that API at setup, insert them into the containerized DB, run our `ComponentSyncService.reconcile()` method, and assert that every component from Sippy has a corresponding valid mapping row.

I'm a mid-level backend developer (2 years Python, basic SQL, no cloud experience) who wants to transition into a cloud/DevOps engineering role within 18 months while keeping my current job. Can you design a detailed learning roadmap for me — but I want you to approach it by first mapping out all the common ways people fail at this transition (burning out from too many certs at once, learning tools without understanding networking fundamentals, skipping hands-on projects, neglecting the cultural/process side of DevOps, etc.), and then structure the plan specifically to avoid each of those failure modes? For each phase of the plan, explicitly call out which failure pattern it's designed to prevent, what the warning signs of that failure look like so I can self-diagnose, and what corrective action to take if I notice myself slipping. I'd also like the plan to account for the fact that I only have about 8-10 hours per week to dedicate to learning.

We just merged a PR into our "StreamDeck" event-driven analytics service (TypeScript, Node 20) that ingests webhook payloads from Stripe, GitHub, and Slack. The problem is the incoming `event` objects are typed as `unknown` and we've been unsafely casting them with `as StripeEvent` etc., which caused a prod bug last night — a malformed GitHub webhook with a missing `action` field slipped through and crashed the handler. I need two things: first, refactor the event ingestion layer to use proper custom type guard functions (e.g., `function isStripeEvent(payload: unknown): payload is StripeEvent`) that validate the shape of each webhook payload at runtime before routing, including nested discriminated unions for sub-event types like `checkout.session.completed` vs `invoice.payment_failed`. Second, since this was a production bug and we're also adding new behavior with these guards, update our living docs — log the webhook crash bug and its fix in the team guide's bug list, add a dev changelog entry describing the type guard refactor, note an idea I had about eventually generating these guards automatically from each provider's OpenAPI spec in the ideas doc, and add a task for next session to write integration tests that send malformed payloads against all the new guards.

Our DJ collective "PulseShift" runs a website where we showcase our custom MIDI mappings for Pioneer DDJ controllers with Rekordbox. We need to overhaul a few things simultaneously. First, we have a Node.js tool that programmatically generates Rekordbox-compatible CSV files for MIDI mappings — it takes a JSON config describing knob/fader/button assignments (channel, CC/Note numbers, min/max ranges) and outputs the CSV with the correct column headers and function references that Rekordbox's MIDI Learn import expects. Right now it handles basic transport controls and EQ knobs for the DDJ-400, but we need to extend it to support the DDJ-1000's four-deck layout including the full effects section mapping (Beat FX Select, Beat FX Level/Depth, Beat FX On/Off per deck) and the correct Rekordbox function names from the official reference. Second, we need a comprehensive Bun test suite for this CSV generator — unit tests that verify correct CSV column ordering and quoting, integration tests that validate generated CSVs against Rekordbox's expected format (including edge cases like function names with special characters and MIDI channel 10 percussion note conflicts), mock tests for the file I/O layer, and all of this wired into our GitHub Actions CI with a minimum 90% coverage threshold that blocks merges if it drops. Third, while we're at it, our website needs maintenance: we're migrating the mapping download pages from our old subdomain to the main domain, need to set up proper 301 redirects so existing links from DJ forums don't break, update our SSL certificates that expire next week, and configure caching headers for the CSV download endpoints so browsers don't serve stale mapping files after we push updates. Can you walk me through all three workstreams with actual code and config examples?

Our marketing team just finished a new set of promotional banners, social media templates, and localized landing page mockups for our "Pinnacle Gear" outdoor apparel brand launch across EN, FR, DE, and JA markets. I need two things done: First, I want to automate publishing these assets to our GitHub repo (`pinnacle-gear/campaign-assets`) with proper release tags using the `gh` CLI, but when I try running `gh auth login` on our new CI runner (Ubuntu 24.04), I get a "command not found" error, and on my Mac I'm getting a 401 when trying to push a release — can you walk me through getting `gh` properly installed and authenticated on both environments so we can script the release? Second, before we push anything, I need you to help me build a QA checklist we can run against all the creative assets — specifically checking that every banner and template follows our brand guidelines (correct Pinnacle Gear logo placement, approved color palette #1B3A4B / #F5A623 / #FFFFFF), meets WCAG 2.1 AA accessibility standards for contrast and alt text, and that all localized versions have correct translations, proper date/number formatting per locale, and no truncated text in the FR/DE/JA variants. Can you give me the full setup walkthrough and then the checklist?

Before I dive back into refactoring the authentication module for our "VaultPass" password manager app, can you search through our previous conversations to find what we decided about the token refresh strategy and the session timeout duration? I remember we debated between sliding window expiration and fixed TTL a few weeks ago and settled on one approach, but I can't remember which — and I want to make sure the code I write today matches what we agreed on.

We're building "RSSVibe," a Swift/SwiftUI RSS reader app targeting international markets. I need two things done together: First, design a RESTful API hierarchy for our backend — we need endpoints for managing feeds, articles, categories, and user preferences, using TypedResults for consistent response typing, with proper documentation comments and versioned paths. Second, for the SwiftUI client consuming this API, all user-facing strings (error messages from API responses, feed category names, empty state descriptions, button labels, etc.) need to be fully localized using `LocalizedStringResource` and `.xcstrings` String Catalogs instead of the old `Localizable.strings` approach. I want type-safe localization keys organized by feature module so our translators can work independently. Can you sketch out the API endpoint design with sample TypedResults return types, and then show the corresponding Swift client layer where every UI string — including dynamically constructed ones like "You have \(count) unread articles in \(feedName)" — uses the new String Catalog workflow with proper pluralization rules and interpolation?

Set up a reusable component library for our internal project management tool "TaskForge" using Next.js and Tailwind CSS with shadcn/ui as the foundation. We need a custom design token system with our brand colors (primary: #1E40AF, secondary: #9333EA, surface: #F8FAFC, destructive: #DC2626), consistent spacing scale, and typography tokens that map to Tailwind's config. Build out these components: 1) A `KanbanCard` component with priority badges (P0-P3) that use color-coded tokens, assignee avatars, due date chips, and subtle hover/focus ring states for accessibility — it needs to look good at both compact and expanded sizes. 2) A `SprintSidebar` with collapsible sections, active state indicators, and keyboard navigation support. 3) A responsive `DashboardHeader` with a command palette trigger, breadcrumbs, and a notification bell with a count badge. For all components, make sure we're using CSS custom properties as design tokens that feed into `tailwind.config.ts` so we can support light/dark mode toggling without duplicating classes everywhere. Also include proper `aria-` attributes, focus-visible rings using our token system, and ensure the color contrast ratios meet WCAG AA. Show me the tailwind config, the CSS token layer, and the three components.

I just finished the "Migrate auth service to OAuth2" task in our project. Can you mark it as done in `todo.md` by moving it from the "In Progress" section to "Completed", and simultaneously add a dated entry in `changelog.md` under a new "## [Unreleased]" section noting that the OAuth2 migration for the auth service is complete? Make sure both files are updated together so we don't end up with one reflecting the change and the other not.

Our company "HarborLink" is a mid-size freight forwarding and customs brokerage firm handling import, export, and re-export flows across Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and the EU. We want to build an internal automation playbook that maps out every repetitive pain point in our current workflow — from booking confirmations and bill of lading generation, to customs classification lookups, denied party screening, duty drawback filing for re-exports, and final-mile delivery scheduling. For each pain point, recommend specific automation tools or scripts (Python preferred) we can bundle together, and include separate workflow diagrams for our three main verticals: (1) perishable goods import into the EU under SPS regulations, (2) electronics re-export through Dubai free zones, and (3) textile manufacturing supply chain from Vietnam to US retailers under USMCA/Section 301 tariff scenarios. Also outline how we should package these automations as a repeatable service offering we can sell to our smaller freight clients.

We're about to split our monorepo project "ClimateLens" (a climate data visualization platform) into two independently deployable services — a Rust ingestion pipeline and a Python/FastAPI analytics API — and we want to manage this transition using SpecWeave. Right now everything lives under a single `spec.md` and `tasks.md`, but after the split each service will have its own release cadence, its own set of living docs, and potentially divergent API contracts that downstream dashboard consumers depend on. I need help designing the increment structure and naming conventions so that cross-service breaking changes (like a schema migration in the ingestion pipeline that ripples into the analytics API's query layer and then into the frontend's caching assumptions) are tracked as linked increments with explicit dependency edges rather than silently drifting apart. Specifically: how should we structure the source-of-truth files and post-task-completion hooks so that completing an increment in one service automatically flags dependent increments in the other as "blocked-needs-review," and what conventions should the `tasks.md` entries follow so that a future engineer reading the history can trace the second- and third-order impacts of any given change — for example, if we change the NetCDF chunking strategy in ingestion, it affects not just the analytics query performance but also the CDN cache hit rates for the public tile server two hops downstream?

We're a Series B startup called "FieldPulse" building a field service management platform (React Native mobile app + Node.js/Express backend on AWS). Our main competitor, ServiceTitan, just announced AI-powered dispatching and predictive maintenance features at their annual conference, and two smaller rivals (Housecall Pro and Jobber) both shipped integrated payment processing last quarter. I need you to use Claude Code in non-interactive mode to scan our entire codebase — specifically the `/services/dispatch`, `/services/scheduling`, and `/services/payments` directories — and produce a detailed competitive gap analysis: map our current feature set against ServiceTitan, Housecall Pro, and Jobber across dispatching intelligence, payment processing, customer communication, and reporting/analytics. For each gap identified, have it generate concrete implementation recommendations with estimated effort (S/M/L t-shirt sizing), flag any architectural limitations in our current code that would block us from reaching parity, and rank the gaps by strategic impact using a weighted scoring model that factors in market demand signals, implementation feasibility from the codebase scan, and differentiation potential. Output everything into a `competitive-roadmap.md` in our repo root with a SWOT matrix, feature comparison table, and a prioritized 6-month engineering roadmap that shows where we should invest to build sustainable advantages rather than just playing catch-up.

I just took a bunch of raw Playwright screenshots of our new "Meridian" dashboard for a blog post walkthrough, and they look pretty rough as-is. Can you write me an ImageMagick script that takes each screenshot PNG from a folder, adds 20px padding, rounds the corners with a 12px radius, applies a subtle drop shadow (offset 4px down, 6px blur, semi-transparent black), and composites the result onto a soft linear gradient background going from #1a1a2e to #16213e? I want the final images to be 1200px wide with consistent sizing so they look polished when embedded in our Hugo blog. Bonus if you can batch-process the whole `screenshots/` directory and output to `polished/`.

Can you review and refactor this Python module that handles our "VaultKeeper" secrets management service? It's grown organically over two years and has become a tangled mess — there's a 600-line `SecretsEngine` class that handles encryption, key rotation, access policy enforcement, audit logging, and caching all in one place, with duplicated retry logic scattered across methods and zero tests. I want you to break it apart following solid design principles — think single responsibility, clear abstractions, minimal coupling — and flag any code smells like premature optimization, cargo-cult patterns, or places where we're reinventing what the standard library already provides. Also, wherever you extract a new class or module, add docstrings that explain *why* the boundary exists, not just *what* the code does, so the next developer understands the intent. Finally, sketch out a testing strategy for the refactored code: what should be unit tested vs integration tested, where to use fakes vs mocks, and how to keep the test suite fast enough that people actually run it before pushing.

Our documentation team maintains an Obsidian vault with markdown articles covering emerging web technologies. I need two things done: First, research the current state of the WASM Component Model and its 2025 tooling ecosystem — specifically what's changed with `wasm-tools`, the new `wasi-http` 0.3 proposal, and how Spin 3.0 and Wasmtime 2025 releases fit together — since this stuff is evolving faster than our docs can keep up. Second, take the resulting research summary (which will be structured as a markdown article with `#`/`##`/`###` headers, **bold** key terms, and `>` blockquotes for important callouts) and convert it into our XML publishing format where headers map to nested `<section level="N">` elements, bold text becomes `<emphasis>` tags, and blockquotes become `<callout>` elements. We publish these to our developer portal's XML feed. Can you handle both the research and the conversion in one pass?

I've been writing a screenplay in Fountain format using VS Code with the Better Fountain extension, and now my producer needs delivery files. Can you walk me through exporting it to both a properly formatted PDF and a Final Draft .fdx file? I'd also like to generate an HTML preview I can share with the director via a link. I'm open to using afterwriting CLI or Highland — whatever gets the cleanest output. The script is called "Vanishing Tides.fountain" and lives in my project root.

My Python training pipeline `run_training.sh` keeps spawning zombie GPU workers that hog VRAM even after the main script crashes. Can you write me a bash script that: (1) lists all processes matching `python.*train` and any associated child processes, (2) checks their GPU memory usage via `nvidia-smi`, (3) gracefully kills any that have been running longer than 6 hours, and (4) restarts my training inside a new tmux session called `gpu-train` with proper logging to `/var/log/training/` so I can detach and check back later? Also, add a cron-compatible watchdog mode that checks every 15 minutes if the tmux session died and relaunches it.

We have a Rails 7 app called "DispatchHub" for coordinating field service technicians. Right now, when a dispatcher assigns a new job to a technician, the technician has to manually refresh their dashboard to see it. We want to add live updates so that when a dispatcher creates or reassigns a work order, every technician's browser dashboard instantly reflects the change — new jobs should slide into their queue in real time, and if a job gets reassigned away from them it should disappear. We also need a small "typing indicator" style presence feature on each work order detail page so dispatchers can see which technicians are currently viewing a given job. Can you walk me through the full implementation — setting up the connection, creating the appropriate channels (one for the per-technician job queue and one for the per-work-order presence), the server-side broadcasting from the WorkOrder model callbacks, the JavaScript subscriptions on the client, and any authentication/authorization considerations for making sure technicians only receive their own jobs? We're using Turbo but want to understand the underlying channel wiring, not just Turbo Streams.

Set up a new TypeScript project for our DeFi arbitrage bot "ArbVault" — I need a BankrClient initialized with two separate wallets: one for gas payments and one for executing trades. The payment wallet should derive its address from a private key stored in a `.env` file, and the trading wallet needs its own separate key configuration. Walk me through the full environment variable setup, the `BankrClient` options object with both wallets wired in, and how to verify each wallet's address after initialization. We're using the Bankr SDK v2.
Also, make sure to include proper error handling in case either wallet fails to initialize — I want to catch and log which specific wallet had the issue. And if you could show how to check the balance of each wallet after setup so we can confirm they're funded before the bot starts running, that would be great. Thanks!
